meaning: Gives every key together with its value, so a loop can use both.
designing so that everyone can use it, including people who see colors differently or read more slowly.
Designed so that everyone can use it, including people who see colors differently.
Joins two conditions. Both must be True: score > 5 and lives > 0.
Adds an item to the end of a list: names.append("Zoe").
The value you put in the brackets when you call a function. In area(3, 4) the arguments are 3 and 4.
Checks that something is True. If it is not, the test fails and shows your message.
Saying who made the art, sound or code you used. Giving credit.
The type for True or False.
Leaves a loop straight away.
A mistake in a program. Every programmer makes them; finding them is part of the fun.
a list of problems found in testing, sorted so the most important ones get fixed first.
A short note: what went wrong, where, and what you changed.
A secret code that shifts every letter along the alphabet by the same amount.
Reading someone’s code to ask questions, find bugs and say what is good.
When two things in a game touch. We check it with distance.
A note for people, after a #. Python ignores it.
Two or more conditions joined with and, or or not.
the part of a game or app that repeats over and over; the smallest version that works.
Deciding what information about people is saved, who can see it, and keeping it safe.
The kind of value: int, float, str or bool. Also just called a type.
Finding and fixing bugs with a strategy: read the traceback, print-debugging, rubber duck.
Breaking a big problem into small parts you can solve one at a time.
a choice you made on purpose, and the reason for it.
A collection that stores values under names (keys): {"lives": 3}.
A comment in triple quotes as the first line of a function, saying what it does.
In pair programming, the person at the keyboard.
A test at the very edge of what is allowed: zero, an empty list, a wall.
Turn a message into secret code / turn it back again.
Scrambling a message so only people with the key can read it.
Something that happens, like a key press, a click or a timer going off.
The function that runs when an event happens.
What the test says should happen, and what really happened.
A string with an f in front that fills in values: f"Score: {score}".
Data saved on the computer, so it is still there after the program stops.
The error you get when you try to read a file that does not exist (yet).
The type for decimal numbers like 3.5.
A drawing of a program’s steps with boxes and arrows.
One tiny step of a game: everything moves a little, then it is drawn.
A named block of code you can use again. Made with def.
visiting projects one by one, like in a museum, and leaving feedback.
The part of a game that runs again and again: move, check, draw.
All the values that describe the game right now: score, lives, positions.
The position of an item in a list. The first item has index 0.
The error you get when you ask for an index that is not in the list.
A loop that never stops. Press the red Stop button.
Checking that what the user typed makes sense, and asking again if not.

The type for whole numbers like 7 or <math display="inline" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><semantics><mrow><mi>−</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">-3</annotation></semantics></math>.
One value inside a list. Also called an element.
The name you use to look up a value in a dictionary.
The error you get when a key is not in the dictionary. Check the spelling!
Tells you how many items are in a list (or letters in a string).
The rules for using someone’s work / giving them credit for it.
A collection of values in order: ["red", "blue"].
Makes the turtle window pay attention to the keyboard.
a checkpoint on the way to the finished project, like M2 “core loop works”.
How a file is opened: "r" read, "w" write (starts empty), "a" append (adds to the end).
In pair programming, the person who reads the task, thinks ahead and spots bugs.
A loop inside another loop. Great for grids and pixel art.
Python’s word for “nothing”. A function with no return gives back None.
A test with ordinary, everyday values.
Turns True into False and False into True.
A bug where a number is one too big or one too small, like using len as the last index.
Tells turtle which function to run when a key is pressed.
Tells turtle to run a function after some milliseconds.
open gets a file ready to use; with closes it again automatically.
Permission from a creator that lets others use their work, often if they give credit.
Joins two conditions. At least one must be True.
A name in a function’s brackets that receives a value: def area(width, height).
Anything that tells who or where you are: real name, address, school, birthday, photos.
a short talk that explains what your project is and why it is interesting.
Letting someone try your game while you watch and take notes.
small finishing touches that make a working program clearer and nicer to use.
Adding print lines to see what your variables hold.
Planning a program in plain words before writing Python.
A tool that finds your test_ functions and runs them all.
Picks one random item from a list.
The modes "r", "w" and "a": look, replace everything, or add to the end.
Hands a value back from a function to the code that called it.
The value a function hands back.
Explaining your code line by line out loud (to a toy or a friend) until you spot the bug.
Where a variable can be used. Variables made inside a function stay inside it.
an event where makers show their work and explain it.
Cuts a string into a list of words: "a b".split() gives ["a", "b"].
The type for text, written in quotes: "hello".
Removes spaces and new-line characters from both ends of a string.
A small function that checks your code works, using assert.
A table on paper where you write how variables change, step by step.
The error report Python shows. Read the last line first.
The error you get when you mix types that do not fit, like "5" + 5.
A piece of data, like 7, "hi" or True. In a dictionary, what is stored under a key.
A name that stores a value. Choose clear names like lives, not x.
one stage of a project; version 2 is the next, improved one.
Repeats while a condition is True. Something inside must change so it can stop.
Opens a file and closes it again safely when the block ends.
